blocks.content: Every request that reaches your backend has to survive a gauntlet before it ever touches the code that actually fetches an order, processes a payment, or returns a profile. Something has to log it. Something has to check whether the caller is even allowed to be there. Something has to make sure it is not the six hundredth request from the same client in the last second.

None of that is the job of the handler that knows how to fetch an order. This topic is about the gauntlet itself, the ordered chain of independent checks a request walks through before it ever reaches its real destination.
1. Introduction & Why It Matters

Think about everything that has to happen before a web request actually reaches the code that fetches an order, processes a payment, or returns a user profile. The request needs to be logged. The caller needs to be authenticated. Maybe the request rate needs to be checked so one client cannot hammer your server. None of that work is the job of the handler that actually knows how to fetch an order.

A middleware is exactly that piece of work, pulled out of the handler and given its own small, focused unit that runs before the real handler ever sees the request. Chain enough of these together and you get a pipeline: the request walks through logging, then authentication, then rate limiting, then finally reaches the handler that was written to do one thing and one thing only.

Without middleware, every handler in your codebase ends up duplicating the same five or six cross-cutting checks, or worse, some handlers remember to check authentication and others quietly forget. Pulling that logic into an ordered chain of independent, reusable middlewares means each concern is written exactly once, and every handler automatically benefits from it.
2. Real-Life Analogy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889843045-39602955.png
blocks.alt: Airport security checkpoint sequence: bag scan, ID check, boarding pass check

blocks.content: Picture an airport security checkpoint. You do not walk straight from the terminal entrance to your gate. First your bag goes through the scanner. Pass that, and an officer checks your ID against your boarding pass. Pass that, and a gate agent scans your boarding pass one final time before you are allowed down the jet bridge. Each of those checkpoints is independent, run by a different system, checking a completely different thing, and each one has the power to stop you from going any further, no matter how the earlier checkpoints went.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889845034-601289496.png
blocks.alt: Office building security doors, each requiring a different badge scan

blocks.content: A large office building works the same way. Swipe your badge at the lobby turnstile to get past the front door. Swipe again to call an elevator that will actually stop on your floor. Swipe a third time at your own floor door to get past that final barrier. Every door only cares about one thing, whether your badge is authorized for that specific door, and any single door refusing your badge stops you right there, well before you reach your desk.
3. Problem It Solves & Definition

Handlers written without middleware tend to grow a familiar shape: many lines of logging, authentication, and validation boilerplate at the top, followed by the two or three lines that actually matter. Copy that handler forty more times for forty more endpoints and the same boilerplate is duplicated forty times, each copy one missed check away from a security bug. Middleware solves this by extracting each concern into its own independent unit that can be reused, reordered, and tested completely separately from the business logic it protects.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.content: A middleware is a function or object that intercepts a request on its way to a final handler, is given the chance to inspect or modify the request or the response, and then either passes control forward to the next middleware in the chain or short-circuits the chain entirely and returns early.
4. Key Terminology

["Middleware: a small, independent unit of code that intercepts a request before it reaches its final handler.","Chain: the ordered sequence of middlewares a request passes through, one after another.","next: the reference a middleware calls to hand control forward to whatever comes next in the chain.","Short-circuiting: a middleware choosing not to call next, stopping the request from ever reaching the rest of the chain.","Handler: the final destination at the end of the chain, the code that actually fulfills the request."]
items: Middleware: a small, independent unit of code that intercepts a request before it reaches its final handler.
Chain: the ordered sequence of middlewares a request passes through, one after another.
next: the reference a middleware calls to hand control forward to whatever comes next in the chain.
Short-circuiting: a middleware choosing not to call next, stopping the request from ever reaching the rest of the chain.
Handler: the final destination at the end of the chain, the code that actually fulfills the request.

blocks.content: 5. Visual Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889846586-996551922.png
blocks.alt: Request flowing through LoggingMiddleware, AuthMiddleware, and the final handler

blocks.content: A Request object enters on the left and is handed to LoggingMiddleware first. LoggingMiddleware does its job and calls next, handing the same request to AuthMiddleware. If AuthMiddleware is satisfied, it calls next too, and the request finally reaches the Handler, which builds the response. If AuthMiddleware is not satisfied, it returns its own rejection immediately, and the Handler never runs at all.
6. Syntax & Code Example

Every middleware in this pattern implements the same tiny contract: a handle method that takes a request plus a next reference. Calling next continues the chain. Not calling it stops the chain right there, and whatever that middleware returns instead becomes the final outcome.

["A Request object that carries whatever data flows through the chain, including anything one middleware sets for a later one to read.","A shared Middleware shape, every implementation exposes a single handle method taking the request and a next reference.","A next reference, a plain callback in this example, that a continuing middleware calls to hand control forward.","A chain runner that walks the list of middlewares in order, feeding each one a next that simply advances to the following one."]
items: A Request object that carries whatever data flows through the chain, including anything one middleware sets for a later one to read.
A shared Middleware shape, every implementation exposes a single handle method taking the request and a next reference.
A next reference, a plain callback in this example, that a continuing middleware calls to hand control forward.
A chain runner that walks the list of middlewares in order, feeding each one a next that simply advances to the following one.

If it fails, it prints a rejection and returns immediately without ever calling next, which is exactly what short-circuits the chain.","MiddlewareChain execute tracks a single index and recurses by calling itself with index plus one wrapped inside a small function, so each middleware only ever sees one next callback, never the whole list.","main builds one chain and reuses it twice, once with a valid token and once without one, which is exactly how a real server reuses one wired chain across every incoming request."]

AuthMiddleware checks the token first. If it fails, it prints a rejection and returns immediately without ever calling next, which is exactly what short-circuits the chain.

9. Behind the Scenes (How next Actually Works)
blocks.text: 9. Behind the Scenes (How next Actually Works)

blocks.content: 9.1 next Is a Closure Over the Rest of the Chain
blocks.text: 9.1 next Is a Closure Over the Rest of the Chain

blocks.content: A middleware never sees the whole list of remaining middlewares, and it never needs to. The chain runner bundles everything that comes after the current middleware, whether that is three more middlewares or the final handler, into a single callable next. Calling it once is enough to advance the entire rest of the chain.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889851453-534090930.png
blocks.alt: Call stack entering each middleware through next and unwinding back out afterward

blocks.content: This is why LoggingMiddleware can print something both before and after next. Entering next pushes deeper into the chain, and only once the final handler has returned does control unwind back out, one middleware at a time, in exactly the reverse order it went in.
9.2 Building the Chain Once, Reusing It For Every Request
blocks.text: 9.2 Building the Chain Once, Reusing It For Every Request

blocks.content: In a real server, the chain is normally built once, when the application starts up, by registering middlewares in the order they should run. That same wired chain, the same list of middlewares plus the same final handler, then processes every single incoming request. Only the Request object changes between calls, the chain structure itself stays exactly the same.
10. Real-World Use Cases & Industry Examples

["E-commerce: a checkout request passes through cart validation middleware and inventory lock middleware before ever reaching the order creation handler.","Banking: a funds transfer request passes through fraud detection middleware and daily limit middleware before the transfer handler ever moves any money.","Social Media: a new post request passes through content moderation middleware and spam detection middleware before the publish handler makes it visible to anyone.","Gaming: a multiplayer move request passes through anti cheat middleware and lag compensation middleware before the game server handler applies it to the match."]
items: E-commerce: a checkout request passes through cart validation middleware and inventory lock middleware before ever reaching the order creation handler.
Banking: a funds transfer request passes through fraud detection middleware and daily limit middleware before the transfer handler ever moves any money.
Social Media: a new post request passes through content moderation middleware and spam detection middleware before the publish handler makes it visible to anyone.
Gaming: a multiplayer move request passes through anti cheat middleware and lag compensation middleware before the game server handler applies it to the match.

blocks.content: The exact same chain shape shows up everywhere, only the specific middlewares change:

blocks.alt: The same middleware chain shape reused across different domains

blocks.content: This exact pattern is also baked directly into some of the most widely used web frameworks in the industry:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889855005-86268969.png
blocks.alt: Express.js request passing through a chain of registered middleware functions

blocks.content: Express.js, one of the most widely used Node.js web frameworks, builds this pattern directly into its core. Every Express application is, at heart, an ordered list of middleware functions registered when the app is configured, and every incoming request walks through that exact list before reaching the route handler that finally sends a response. Spring applications lean on the same idea through their Filter and Interceptor chains, run before a controller ever sees the request.
11. Advantages & Limitations

{"headers":["Advantages","Limitations"],"rows":[["Each cross-cutting concern lives in exactly one reusable place instead of being copied into every handler.","A long chain can make it harder to trace exactly which middleware produced a given response without good logging."],["Middlewares can be reordered, added, or removed without touching the final handler at all.","Order matters a great deal, and putting two middlewares in the wrong order can silently break behavior."],["Any middleware can short-circuit the chain early, stopping bad requests before they waste any real work.","A slow or blocking middleware placed early in the chain slows down every single request, even the ones it approves."],["Individual middlewares are small and easy to unit test in isolation from the rest of the chain.","Debugging shared state that one middleware sets and another reads can be confusing if that contract is not documented."]]}
12. Common Mistakes & Best Practices
12.1 Common Mistakes

["Putting authentication after a middleware that already does expensive work, wasting effort on requests that get rejected anyway.","Forgetting that a middleware which never calls next also prevents any response from reaching the caller, unless it sends its own response first.","Sharing mutable state between middlewares through global variables instead of passing it through the request object itself.","Writing one giant middleware that handles logging, authentication, and validation together, instead of several small, independently testable ones."]
items: Putting authentication after a middleware that already does expensive work, wasting effort on requests that get rejected anyway.
Forgetting that a middleware which never calls next also prevents any response from reaching the caller, unless it sends its own response first.
Sharing mutable state between middlewares through global variables instead of passing it through the request object itself.
Writing one giant middleware that handles logging, authentication, and validation together, instead of several small, independently testable ones.

blocks.content: 12.2 Best Practices

["Order middlewares from cheapest check to most expensive, so obviously bad requests get rejected before any real work happens.","Keep every middleware focused on exactly one concern, so it can be reused, tested, and reordered independently of the rest.","Attach data one middleware discovers, like a verified user, directly onto the request object so later middlewares and the handler can read it safely.","Log clearly whenever a middleware short-circuits the chain, since that is usually the most useful place to look when debugging a rejected request."]
items: Order middlewares from cheapest check to most expensive, so obviously bad requests get rejected before any real work happens.
Keep every middleware focused on exactly one concern, so it can be reused, tested, and reordered independently of the rest.
Attach data one middleware discovers, like a verified user, directly onto the request object so later middlewares and the handler can read it safely.
Log clearly whenever a middleware short-circuits the chain, since that is usually the most useful place to look when debugging a rejected request.

blocks.content: 13. Key Takeaways & Cheat Sheet

["A middleware is a small, independent unit that intercepts a request before it reaches its final handler.","Middlewares are chained together, each one calling next to pass control forward, or not calling it to short-circuit the chain.","The same chain instance is usually built once and reused for every incoming request, only the request itself changes.","Ordering matters, since each middleware only sees whatever request state the earlier middlewares left behind.","This pattern is a concrete application of the Chain of Responsibility idea, used everywhere from Express.js to Spring Filter and Interceptor chains."]
items: A middleware is a small, independent unit that intercepts a request before it reaches its final handler.
Middlewares are chained together, each one calling next to pass control forward, or not calling it to short-circuit the chain.
The same chain instance is usually built once and reused for every incoming request, only the request itself changes.
Ordering matters, since each middleware only sees whatever request state the earlier middlewares left behind.
This pattern is a concrete application of the Chain of Responsibility idea, used everywhere from Express.js to Spring Filter and Interceptor chains.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If asked why middleware exists instead of just calling several functions at the top of every handler, the sharpest answer is reuse and ordering: each middleware is written once, can be composed in any order across any set of routes, and can short-circuit the chain the moment it detects a problem, without the handler ever needing to know any of that happened.
